purpose:
This Decision Sheet presents one formal
objection, received in response to the formal advertising of
various traffic calming features on Redcar Lane and Barrows Lane,
Steeton. (as identified within Drawing No. P/HS/THN/105748/CON-OV)
(attached as Appendix A)).
The scheme was developed in response to a fatal collision on Tarn
Lane, along with a number of other serious and slight injury
collisions recorded across this part of the network.
The aim of the scheme is to improve road safety by introducing
revised speed limits and physical speed reducing features where
they are most needed, ensuring that vehicle speeds better reflect
the local environment and creating a safer environment for all road
users.

This report considers the Bingley
Neighbourhood Development Plan (NDP) which has been prepared by
Bingley Town Council. It provides an update following examination
and considers the key procedural milestones ahead.

(1)          
That the submitted Bingley Neighbourhood Development Plan, and
accompanying Policies Map (Appendices 1a and 1b) be subject to the
modifications (Proposed Modifications PM1 to PM9) as set out in the
Examiner’s Report (Appendix 2), together with any relevant
factual changes to ensure the amended Plan is correct.

 

(2)

Plan be subject to a local referendum in the designated
neighbourhood area (the Bingley Town Council area).

Assistant Director (Planning, Transportation and Highways) in

be published one week earlier than currently.

authority to make consequential amendments to the Constitution as a
result of any recommendations approved by Full
Council.

The Director of Legal and Governance.

content:
Resolved –
 

(1)          
That, in the event the Appointments Panel is unable to meet to
conduct the final interviews by the week commencing 25 May 2026,
the Chief Executive be delegated authority to convene an
Appointments Panel for the purpose of concluding the selection
process.

 

(2)          
That the Appointments Panel shall comprise three Elected
Members, including at least one Executive Member. Consideration
will also be given to including representation from Group Leaders
to ensure cross?party continuity throughout the recruitment
process.

 

(3)          
That any decision to appoint a Strategic Director remains the
responsibility of the Elected Member Appointments Panel.
 
Reason for
Decision:
To ensure continuity
of the recruitment process and avoid undue delay in the appointment
of the Strategic Director, while maintaining appropriate
governance, political balance, and Member oversight.
 
Alternative Options
Considered and Rejected:
To defer the
recruitment process until the standard Appointments Panel could
meet - Rejected due to potential operational and strategic impact
arising from a delay in filling the post.
 
To be actioned
by: Chief Executive
 
(Lucy Thompson
– lucy.thompson@bradford.gov.uk)

Under Council Standing Order 9.1.2 a vote was
taken to re-order the business on the agenda to move Motion 11.4
(supporting our local schools: fair pension contribution rates for
Multi Academy Trusts) to be the first motion to be considered.
 
 Resolved-
 
 That under
Council Standing Order 9.1.2 to re-order the business on the agenda
to move Motion 11.4 (supporting our local schools: fair pension
contribution rates for Multi Academy Trusts) to be the first motion
to be considered.
 
11.4    SUPPORTING OUR LOCAL SCHOOLS: FAIR
PENSION     CONTRIBUTION RATES
FOR MULTI ACADEMY TRUSTS
 
As set out in the published agenda Motion 11.4
was moved by Councillor Wheatley and seconded by Councillor
Dearden.
 
In accordance with Council Standing Orders
18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional published papers
Amendment H) was moved by Councillor Thornton and
seconded by Councillor Duffy.
 
Following a number
of speakers in accordance with Council Standing Order 18.12
Amendment H as set out below was put to the vote was carried and
became the substantive Motion, was then voted on and was
carried.
 
 Resolved-
 
That with the
addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion be
amended to read as follows:
 
Council notes:
 

1.            
We have a responsibility to all children in all schools and
settings         across our
district and we take that responsibility seriously.
 

2.            
The majority of schools of all types provide an excellent education
for          
their students while also protecting the pay progression, maternity
      leave, sick
pay and workloads of their staff. We expect all schools to do
   so. Trade unions have long
campaigned against any academy trusts  
that have failed to meet these standards by eroding the pay and
         
conditions of school staff alongside rising CEO pay.
 

3.            
Along with other funds in the Local Government Pension Scheme
       (LGPS)
in England and Wales, West Yorkshire Pension Fund (WYPF)
      has undertaken
a triennial actuarial valuation as at 31 March 2025,    which will set contribution rates for each
employer that participates in       the Fund, for the 3 year
period starting on 1 April 2026.

4.            
The contribution rates for the three years starting 1 April 2026
are       required
to be formalised by 31 March 2026.
 

5.            
WYPF carries out its actuarial valuation in accordance with the
LGPS         regulations
and guidance. Its approach is in line with the majority of
  LGPS funds in England and Wales.
 

6.            
The actuarial assumptions and methodology used by WYPF to
      calculate the
employer contribution rates for academy trusts are identical to
those it uses to calculate the rates for councils.
 

7.            
Due to the consistent strong performance of WYPF, Academy Trusts
     with members in WYPF
will be paying less than academy schools and          
councils in most other areas of England and Wales.
 

8.            
WYPF consulted with all stakeholders on its Funding Strategy
      
Statement from August to October 2025 and received around 160
        
responses, the vast majority from academy trusts. This is by some
margin the most responses to a FSS consultation ever received by a
   LGPS fund. WYPF considered all
the comments from the academies       and their advisers and
approved additional changes to the draft FSS. All these changes
acted to reduce contribution rates for council and for          academy
trusts.
 

9.            
This year (2026-27) employer contributions rates fall by 2.1% of
pay for       
the vast majority of academy trusts.
 

10.         
That councillors cannot instruct WYPF to set a particular
contribution   rate.
 
Council resolves
to:
 
Encourage WYPF to continue their open
engagement with the MATs so that there’s a better mutual
understanding of each other’s position.
 
Request a written response from WYPF to the
Council Leader before the end of the civic year assuring the
council that its approach to employer pension contributions is
equitable and in line with common practice nationally.
 
To be actioned
by:  Director of West Yorkshire Pension
Fund
 
11.1    FAILURE TO DELIVER
CORE NEIGHBOURHOOD SERVICES
As
set out in the published agenda Motion 12.1 was moved by Councillor
Saddiq and seconded by Councillor Elahi.
In accordance
with Council Standing Orders 18.4 and
18.8 an amendment (additional published papers Amendment
A) was moved by Councillor Edwards and seconded by
Councillor Love.
In
accordance with Council Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 a second
amendment (additional published papers Amendment B) was moved
by Councillor Davies and seconded by Councillor
Pollard.
In
accordance with Council Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 a third
amendment (additional published papers Amendment C) was moved
by Councillor Ferriby and seconded by Councillor
Hinchcliffe.
Following
a number of speakers in accordance with Council Standing Order
18.12 Amendment C as set out below was put to the vote was carried
and became the substantive Motion, was then voted on and was
carried.
 Resolved-
That with
the addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion be
amended to read as follows:
This
Council notes:
1. That neighbourhood services
comprise a wide range of vital council services, such as street
cleaning, parks, youth services, supporting community groups,
support for older people, skills and employment support, tackling
antisocial behaviour and supporting community events, among
others.
 
2. Our thanks to the
hardworking staff in our neighbourhoods teams – they care
about their local areas and work with councillors and residents to
get things done.
 
3. That neighbourhood services,
including waste collection, street cleansing and fly-tipping
removal, are among the most basic and statutory functions of a
local authority, required to maintain public health, environmental
quality, community safety and public confidence in local
government.
 
4. Flytipping is a significant
and visible problem across the country, including in the Bradford
district. Whilst fly-tipping continues to be a key priority and
concern for the council and residents, tonnages of illegally
dumped waste have not increased over the last few years.
 
5. The selfish and antisocial
behaviour of those who, outrageously, tip rubbish on public or
private land and that this costs the rest of us
significantly.
 
6. That the Labour
Group’s budget approved by Full Council on 10th
March includes significant new funding to extend enforcement,
including an additional £1m that will clear more gullies, get
rid of more abandoned vehicles and deliver a Day of Action every
single workday of the year. The budget also includes £450,000
for a city centre team to tackle waste and strengthen enforcement,
£150,000 for trees and woodland maintenance, an additional
£350,000 for increased enforcement to tackle housing,
planning and highways issues; and a reduction in the household
charge for bulky waste collections.
 
7. There is inappropriate
behaviour by a minority of residents and non-residents who fail to
dispose of their waste appropriately unlike most residents who use
their recycling and general waste bins, street bins, HWRCs or book
a bulky waste collection, all of which are crucial in keeping the
district tidy. 
 
8. Areas with high levels of
rented properties and therefore more transient populations are
known to face additional challenges in meeting recycling targets.
The Council takes a series of measures to support, educate and
enforce good recycling practices.
 
9. That the council regularly
publicises the need for residents to check that any waste trader
they employ to dispose of their waste has an in-date permit to
trade in waste collection. A list of these is available on the
government website at 
https://environment.data.gov.uk/public-register/view/search-waste-carriers-brokers.
 
10. That the council enforces a
comprehensive range of actions to tackle and prevent litter and
flytipping and continual improvement activity is being implemented,
including CCTV, partnership working with the police, strengthened
intelligence-led enforcement activity, community engagement through
action days and preparatory work for the introduction of food waste
collections to improve recycling performance.
 
11. That the council already
reports comprehensive data, such as details of flytipping offences
and disposal to the cross-party Area Committees and Regeneration
and Environment Overview & Scrutiny Committee, along with other
regular reports on waste services, cleansing and environmental
enforcement.
 
12. That the council checks
every reported incident of flytipping and assesses the
responsibility for clearing it.
 
13. That we encourage and
welcome responsible members of the public to report flytipping
incidents. Individual reports of flytipping are therefore often
reported multiple times, meaning the number of reports outnumber
the actual incidents and amounts cleared.
 
14. That enforcement of
flytipping is reliant on identifiable evidence which is gathered
from the flytip site and is investigated and pursued by the
Enforcement Team, which this council is directing more resourcing
to.
 
15. That missed bin collections
are picked up as soon as possible following the missed date and
collections are often missed due to inconsiderate parking and skips
blocking access to streets, weather conditions or vehicle
breakdowns.
 
The
Council resolves to:
 
1. Continue the work of the
Environmental Enforcement Team including its work with the Police
and VOSA (Vehicle and Operator Services Agency) checking that those
trading in waste collection are registered to do so, that the
vehicles they use are taxed and tested and in bringing to book
those who fly-tip be that through a Fixed Penalty Notice or
prosecution.
 
2. Continue to work with
residents regarding the correct way to dispose of household waste
and recycling and update them of upcoming changes such as Food
Waste Collections.
 
3. Continue our anti-littering
campaigns and our work with Keep Britain Tidy.
 
4. Continue our People Can days
of action working with residents and community groups in keeping
the local environment clean, tidy and litter-free.
 
5. Continue to provide
comprehensive and transparent data to the Area Committees and
Scrutiny committee regarding Waste, Street Cleaning, Fly Tipping
and Cleansing. Ward-level reporting will be accompanied by
contextual indicators such as population density, housing type and
commercial waste activity to prevent misleading
comparisons.
 
To be
actioned by: Strategic Director Environment
 
 
11.2    PROTECTING LOCAL
PUBS AND COMMUNITY SOCIAL SPACES IN BRADFORD DISTRICT
 
As set out in the published
agenda Motion 11.2 was moved by Councillor Edwards and seconded by
Councillor Hickson.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional
published papers Amendment D) was moved by Councillor
Ross-Shaw and seconded by Councillor Hughes.
 
Following a number of speakers in accordance with Council
Standing Order 18.12 Amendment D as set out below was put to the
vote was carried and became the substantive Motion, was then voted
on and was carried.
 
Resolved-
 
That
with the addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion
be amended to read as follows:
 
This
Council notes that:
 

Local pubs and social clubs play a vital role in
community life, providing social spaces that reduce loneliness,
support wellbeing, strengthen neighbourhood identity, and
contribute to the local economy.

Bradford District is home to many renowned pubs and
bars which contribute to the character, culture and economic
vitality of the district. This heritage extends to the brewing
sector, which is home to some of the country’s most cherished
and recognised breweries, including Saltaire Brewery and Timothy
Taylor’s as well as craft breweries like Amity Brew Co moving
their brewery to Idle & Thackley from Leeds.

 

Across the UK, pubs are being lost at an alarming
rate due to conversion or demolition, often permanently removing
valued community assets. Data collected by Campaign for Real Ale
(CAMRA) shows that in the last 12 months alone 366 pubs have been
lost, equivalent to more than one pub every day, through demolition
or conversion to other uses. While the hospitality sector has been
one of the highest growth sectors since the 2008 financial crisis,
the nature of that growth has evolved so traditional pubs may not
necessarily have benefited.
 

 

Pubs face significant financial pressures, including
rising energy and other costs and the longer term impact of the
cost of living crisis on household incomes, which are adding to the
challenges facing the hospitality sector. Many pubs have also been
negatively affected by pubcos or their owners. There has also been
much uncertainty around business rates as the COVID-era support
gradually comes to an end.

 

Bradford District has experienced the loss of valued
local pubs and venues in 2025, including:

 

The Rose & Crown, Westgate, Bradford City
Centre, which closed in March 2025
 

Studio 48 & Groove Pad, Saltaire Road, Shipley,
which closed in October 2025
 

The Roebuck, Skipton Road, Keighley, which closed in
December 2025
 

The loss of pubs has a cumulative negative impact on
communities, particularly in areas where there are few alternative
social or community spaces. It can also damage the local economy
and the vibrancy of the local high street.
 

 

Pubs are frequently targeted for redevelopment due
to their prominent locations and distinctive buildings, even where
they remain viable or could be brought back into use, despite
national planning policy recognising pubs as community assets and
explicitly supporting the retention of community facilities where
they serve a social function.

 

Changing trends require pubs to modernise and evolve
to stay relevant to the communities they serve. For example,
evidence shows more young people don’t drink compared to
their predecessors. In Scotland a study by Stirling University
found road safety based changes to the law on drink driving, to
tackle the 65 deaths caused by legal drink driving every year, saw
little long term economic impact on those pubs that evolved their
low/no alcohol and food offer.
 
This
Council believes that:
 

Local pubs are more than commercial premises. They
are pieces of social infrastructure that contribute to community
cohesion, wellbeing and local economic resilience.

 

Good quality pubs, bars and restaurants,
particularly those led by independent operators, are vital to
supporting and improving the night-time economy across Bradford
District, especially in our city centre, towns and
villages.
 

 
Investing in culture-led
regeneration, from Bradford Live to Keighley Creative and our Towns
Fund programmes in Keighley and Shipley, coupled with our status as
UK City of Culture 2025, supports the growth of the hospitality
sector by delivering quality events, creating jobs, increasing
footfall and driving growth across the district.
 
The permanent loss of pubs can
contribute to social isolation, reduce footfall for surrounding
businesses, and undermine the success of our city and town
centres.
 

Local authorities have a responsibility to use
planning policy, economic development tools and partnership working
to support the retention of valued local facilities wherever
possible.

 

Where pubs are no longer viable as privately run
businesses, alternative models such as community ownership should
be encouraged and supported. This has happened successfully in the
district already, for instance with the Malt Shovel in Menston
being bought by members of the community, and continuing to be at
the heart of the community.
 

 
This
Council resolves to:
 

1.            
Continue and develop our culture-led regeneration
programme, which   will deliver the most
sustainable benefits to the hospitality sector, by    driving jobs, footfall and housing growth in
our urban centres, while          creating
a sustainable UK City of Culture legacy will provide a   permanent lift to our cultural and events
programme, attracting         thousands of
visitors to the district every year.
 

2.            
Request officers provide a paper to the cross-party
Local Plan   Reference Group on how
existing local planning policies are being      applied to pub conversions and
demolitions across the district, and to   consider whether the emerging Local Plan could
include additional         measures to
further protect pubs and community social spaces.
 

3.            
Request the Strategic Director for Growth to look at
the challenges and        opportunities facing
the hospitality sector, including issues such as    access to skills, staffing and local
transport, as part of the Growth and       Skills Partnership. This
review will get direct feedback as part of the     process through a hospitality
roundtable meeting, including landlords, to feed in to Council
policies and strategies such as the Growth and          
Regeneration Plan and the Place Marketing board and any further
   actions as required.
 
To be
actioned by:  Strategic Director
Growth
 
11.3    BRADFORD SUPPORTS A
NATIONAL YEAR OF READING
 
As set out in the published
agenda Motion 11.3 was moved by Councillor Ferriby and seconded by
Councillor Fricker.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional
published papers Amendment E) was moved by Councillor Russell
and seconded by Councillor Caroline Whitaker.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 a second amendment (additional
published papers Amendment F) was moved by Councillor Davies
and seconded by Councillor Pollard.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 a third amendment (additional
published papers Amendment G) was moved by Councillor
Sunderland and seconded by Councillor Naylor.
 
Following a number of speakers in accordance with Council
Standing Order 18.12 Amendments E, F and G were put to the vote and
lost. The Motion as set out below was then put to the vote and was
carried.
 
Resolved-
 
Council notes:
 
Literacy changes everything. It
transforms a person’s opportunities to succeed in
life.
 
Reading provides joy at all
ages and builds connection with each other through
stories.
 
Low literacy is closely linked
to poverty. There is a moral and economic imperative to tackle low
rates of literacy.
 
The education secretary Bridget
Phillipson announced that 2026 will be a National Year of Reading,
an initiative by the Department for Education in collaboration with
the National Literacy Trust.
 
The National Year of Reading
2026 is a campaign to address the steep decline in reading amongst
children, young people and adults.
 
Investing in culture and
learning is key to the council’s strategic objectives to
regenerate the district and boost residents’ opportunities in
life. Reading is also central to the Government’s Plan for
Change: it supports success in school, work and life, boosts
wellbeing, brings people together and increases empathy.
 
The strong presence of the
National Literacy Trust here in the Bradford district.  Since 2014 NLT has worked with over 50,000
children, families and teachers in the district and has given out
over 150,000 books to children.
We have two major literature
festivals in Bradford and Ilkley; the Summer Reading Challenge run
by our libraries; and the daily work of our libraries and of
volunteers, our nursery schools, primary schools and the Book
Trust. Last year the City of Culture team did work with every
secondary school library in the district; as well as work by
Business in the Community; and Dolly Parton’s Imagination
Library among others.
 
Dolly Parton's Imagination
Library has been sending books to children across Bradford
district every month since 2012 with thanks to community partners
in the area. There are over 2,000 children currently
registered in Bradford district, with over 1,100 of these
registered with Keighley Imagination Library, making it the
12th largest Imagination Library in the UK. 
 
This council has delivered
significant recent investments in our libraries, including a
refurbishment of 10 council libraries to make them modern, flexible
and accessible spaces. Work is currently ongoing with partners to
deliver the best library solution for Baildon and the City Centre
library facilities.
 
Education results are improving
in our district. The latest figures just released for last year
show that primary schools’ results across the Bradford
district have improved and are closer to pre-pandemic levels.
Reading is a cornerstone of early education, and the Year of
Reading is an opportunity to support this progress.
 
Council resolves to:
 
Sign the Local Authority pledge
to support the National Year of Reading 2026 by:

Using our
communications channels to share key messages and spread awareness
about the initiative

 

Convening partners
such as schools, early years settings and higher and further
education providers to support the Year of Reading
Encouraging
volunteers, including the council’s own workforce, to take
part in the Year of Reading

 

Continuing to invest
in and support our fantastic libraries across the
district

 

Launching a new
communications drive for library memberships, publicising the
benefits of free books and the range of other services provided in
our libraries and community hubs.

 
To be
actioned by:  Acting Strategic Director
Children’s Services
 
Under Council Standing Order
9.1.2 a vote was taken to re-order the business on the agenda to
move Motion 11.8 (youth matters in Bradford) to be the first motion
to be considered.
 
Resolved-
 
That
under Council Standing Order 9.1.2 to re-order the business on the
agenda to move Motion 11.8 (youth matters in Bradford) to be the

11.8    YOUTH MATTERS IN
BRADFORD
 
As set out in the published
agenda Motion 11.8 was moved by Councillor Faiz Ilyas and seconded
by Councillor Kamran Hussain.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional
published papers Amendment N) was moved by Councillor Saddiq
and seconded by Councillor Saleem.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 a second amendment (additional
published papers Amendment O) was moved by Councillor Watson
and seconded by Councillor Brown.
 
Following a number of speakers in accordance with Council
Standing Order 18.12 Amendments N and O were put to the vote and
lost. The Motion as set out below was then put to the vote and was
carried.
Bradford Council notes that:
 
Youth Matters is the new
national youth strategy published in December 2025. It calls
for:
 
o        Trusted adults
and a skilled youth workforce
o        Safe,
welcoming places to go
o        Improved
mental health and wellbeing support
o        Stronger youth
voice and participation
o        Better access
to skills, work and opportunities
o        A shift from
fragmented services to joined up, locally led delivery 
In Bradford we want to listen
as well as lead and make sure that every young person knows that
this council believes in them, stands with them and is prepared to
do the hard work required to help them
thrive.
 
Recent research by YMCA England
& Wales found that over the past 14 years, local authority
funding for youth services in England has fallen by 76% in real
terms, representing a loss of £1.3 billion since
2010/11.
 
Many councils across the
country cut their youth service entirely in response to the Tory
and Liberal Democrat austerity cuts from 2010 to 2024, but
Bradford’s Labour-led council in contrast maintained
significant funding for our youth services.
 
The publication of Youth
Matters: Your National Youth Strategy - the first dedicated youth
strategy in 20 years - provides an opportunity to reset
how national ambition is translated into local delivery for the
next 10 years.
The Strategy recognises local
authorities as key partners in shaping youth services, coordinating
local offers and ensuring funding reaches communities where it can
have the greatest impact.
 
Bradford has: 
 

One of the youngest
populations in the country 


Deeply rooted
community, voluntary and faith sector youth
provision 


Existing work under
way through early help, youth justice, safeguarding partnerships,
violence reduction, SEND services and neighbourhood
initiatives.
Developed a new
Children and Young People’s Strategy 2025-35, enabling annual
monitoring of district-wide outcomes for all children and young
people, and termly monitoring of five priority areas of
work.

 
 Bradford Council
resolves: 
 

To publicly
welcome the ambition of Youth Matters: Your National Youth
Strategy through this motion and commit to its delivery in
partnership with government and other partners. 

 

To request that the
Acting Strategic Director for Children’s Services works with
the Assistant Director for Communities, the Director of Public
Health, the Children and Families Trust and the relevant portfolio
holders and our partners, to ensure that delivery of our new
Children and Young People’s Strategy is aligned with the
national Youth Matters strategy.

 

To commit to
strengthening youth voice locally by expanding meaningful
co-production with young people and supporting young people to
engage confidently in local democracy, youth forums, school
councils and community groups.

 

To welcome this
Labour Council’s enduring and now increasing commitment to
youth services across the district.

 

To work with partners
to rebuild access to safe, vibrant, welcoming and accessible places
to go, including youth centres, community and youth hubs,
libraries, sports and cultural spaces.

 

To prioritise trusted
adults and the youth workforce by: 


Supporting training,
retention and progression of youth workers and
mentors 


Strengthening
partnership working between schools, youth services,
health, police and the voluntary sector 


Recognising our
long-held position of youth work as a preventative public service,
not an optional extra. 

 

To press Government
to deliver fair, long-term funding to deliver the aims of Youth
Matters that reflects Bradford’s scale of need and
youth population. 

 

To ask for regular
reporting to the Children and Young People’s Executive and to
members at Overview & Scrutiny and Area Committees on
progress, challenges and outcomes in our Children and
Young People’s Strategy and local work contributing to
delivery of Youth Matters. 

 
To be
actioned by:  Acting Strategic Director
Children’s Services, Strategic Director Growth, Interim
Strategic Director Environment and Director of Public
Health
 
11.5    IMPROVING RECYCLING
PERFORMANCE AND ACCESS TO          
HOUSEHOLD WASTE RECYCLING FACILITIES
 
As set out in the published
agenda Motion 11.5 was moved by Councillor Loy and seconded by
Councillor Poulsen.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 an amendment (additional
published papers Amendment I) was moved by Councillor Brown
and seconded by Councillor Brown.
 
In accordance with Council
Standing Orders 18.4 and 18.8 a second amendment (additional
published papers Amendment J) was moved by Councillor Ferriby
and seconded by Councillor Hinchcliffe.
 
Following a number of speakers in accordance with Council
Standing Order 18.12 Amendment J as set out below was put to the
vote was carried and became the substantive Motion, was then voted
on and was carried.
 
Resolved-
That
with the addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion
be amended to read as follows:
 
Council notes:
 
The council recognises the
importance of improving recycling performance across the district
and ensuring residents have appropriate access to recycling
facilities. Increasing recycling rates is a key part of
Bradford’s wider waste strategy and will also support the
council in meeting forthcoming national requirements under the
Government’s Simpler Recycling reforms.
 
The Executive’s recent
decision to reduce the charge for bulky waste collections to
support households with the cost of living and make it easier to
dispose of excess waste.
 
Bradford Council currently
spends approximately £38 million per year delivering
household waste collection, recycling and disposal services across
the district. These services continue to operate within a
challenging financial environment as the country recovers from 14
years of Conservative austerity cuts and the council must balance
environmental ambitions with the need to manage costs
effectively.
 
The council is due to receive
£13.6m of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) funding in
2026-27 although this amount is not guaranteed for future
years.   The sum will decline
rapidly as producers remove packaging from the supply
chain.
 
Of this the council is planning
to invest £5.9m of the EPR funding in 2026/27 to support
measures aimed at improving recycling performance and preparing for
the implementation of the Government’s Simpler Recycling
reforms.
 
The remaining
£7.7 million of EPR funding will be used to offset the
wider costs associated with managing household packaging waste
– the very reason this funding has become available. Given
the significant financial pressures facing the council, this
funding will be used to support the overall cost of delivering the
waste service, which remains a substantial financial commitment for
the authority.
 
Tory austerity cuts over 14
years forced councils across the country to reduce their service
provision and the size of their operations.
 
In 2022 the council’s
HWRC service provision was benchmarked against authorities with
socio-demographic similarities, measured using a nearest-neighbour
rank, which found that Bradford had the highest number of HWRCs per
100,000 population (1.5 sites) when compared with its neighbouring
authorities.
 
Bradford now has 0.9 HWRC sites
per 100,000 residents which is above the level of most comparable
local authorities.
The council continues to
monitor recycling performance and service accessibility across the
district and will consider options for improving recycling
infrastructure and service delivery as part of the wider waste
transformation programme.
 
Any future proposals relating
to further investment in recycling infrastructure would need to be
considered alongside the council’s financial position,
statutory duties and wider environmental objectives in the
budget.
 
Council resolves to:
 
Ask the Interim Strategic
Director of Environment to bring forward a report to Executive at
the earliest opportunity outlining plans for food waste collections
and improvements to the customer offer.
 
Work with residents to further
improve recycling rates including:
 

Introducing a food
waste collection service
Education and
engagement programmes to support behaviour change and increase
recycling participation
Enforcement
activity to tackle misuse of waste services and address
fly-tipping
Operational
improvements linked to the Council’s wider waste
transformation programme

 
To be
actioned by:  Interim Strategic Director
of Environment
 
TOURIST “TAX” IMPACT ON LOCAL TOURISM, BUSINESSES
AND FAMILIES
The voting on Motion 11.6 was
as follows:
 
Amendment L was put to the vote
and lost
 
Amendment K as set out below
was put to the vote and was carried and became the substantive
Motion, was then voted on and was carried.
 
Resolved-
 
That
with the addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion
be amended to read as follows:
 
Council notes:
 

The
Government’s announcement in the November 2025 Budget that
Mayors of Strategic Authorities will be permitted to issue a
Visitor Levy on overnight stays.

 

The announcement is
the latest step forward in the government’s mission to
devolve power and give those who know their areas best the control
over how money is spent in their communities. It gives local areas
a new power to raise and invest funds free from central government
diktat.

 

The move would ensure
UK mayors have the same powers as their counterparts in many other
countries such as France, Italy and the US where charges on
short-term trips are already commonplace.

 

Any new levy would
apply to visitors at accommodation providers including hotels,
holiday lets, bed and breakfasts, and guesthouses.

 

Funds raised could
then help fund local projects that improve communities and enhance
tourists’ experiences, that could potentially help attract
more visitors – without needing approval from central
government. Any region that opts out of the levy will be left
without these significant funds to invest on a local level, which
other places will benefit from.

 

In West Yorkshire the
Mayor could invest these significant funds in priorities that
strengthen both the visitor economy and our broader regional growth
objectives. This could include: transport infrastructure
improvements that enhance connectivity to visitor attractions,
regeneration of public realm; business support programmes for the
hospitality sector; skills and training for the tourism sector;
visitor experience improvements; product development (such as
itineraries); destination marketing to promote the region; overall
destination management, and investment in events that drive
economic activity during periods of lower demand.

 

The government ran a
consultation which ran until 18th February, giving all
stakeholders, businesses and the public the chance to have their
say.

 

In 2003 Manchester
became the first UK city to launch a so-called tourist tax for
visitors. It was not the government that promoted this tax but
rather the hotel industry itself, which identified the opportunity
of using the tax revenue to boost the tourism economy. A study
published in Tourism Management found that the tax introduced in
Manchester had no significant effect on hotel performance during
the first 18 months after its implementation. The tax generated
£2.8m from overnight visitors in its first year which is
being reinvested in Manchester.

 

In their recent
council budget proposal, the opposition Conservative group on
Bradford Council proposed their own tourist and resident tax of an
additional £2 tax on theatre tickets.

 
Council resolves:
 

To work with the
Mayor of West Yorkshire to make the most of this opportunity to
invest significant funds in our district, supporting our economic
growth strategy and our work to further improve our district as a
visitor destination.

 

To back the Mayor who
is asking government for flexibilities to be put in place so we can
decide locally about which relevant exemptions to put in place,
such as children’s residentials and scout trips so that they
would not be impacted in any way.

 

For the Council
Leader to ask the Mayor to ensure that Bradford district locations
that receive large numbers of tourists - for example Haworth,
Ilkley, Shipley Glen tramway, the city centre and others - benefit
from reinvestment of the funds raised.

 
To be
actioned by: Leader of Council
 
11.7    PROTECTING AND
ENHANCING BLUE AND GREEN          
INFRASTRUCTURE IN IDLE AND THACKLEY WARD
         
Amendment M as set out below
was put to the vote and was carried and became the substantive
Motion, was then voted on and was carried.
 
Resolved-
 
That
with the addition and deletion of the appropriate words, the motion
be amended to read as follows:
 
This
Council notes:
 
1. Bradford has many blue and
green infrastructure assets, including our world famous moorland,
part of a number of sites making up the Bradford Pennine Gateway
National Nature Reserve, five Green Flag parks and also many local
amenities in every corner of our district.
 
2. Idle and Thackley ward is a
good example of this, containing significant blue and green
infrastructure assets including Buck Wood, Idle Recreation Ground,
the River Aire corridor and the Leeds and Liverpool Canal
corridor.
 
3. These assets provide
essential functions including flood mitigation, biodiversity and
habitat connectivity, climate resilience, recreational
opportunities and walking and cycling connectivity for
residents.
 
4. Traditional dry-stone walls
across the district form part of our historic landscape character
and field patterns and contribute to biodiversity, drainage and the
visual identity of the area.
 
5. Despite significant
investment across the district, existing walking and cycling routes
- including canal towpaths, woodland paths and pedestrian links
between neighbourhoods - can be inconsistently connected and
variably maintained.
6. The Council has declared a
climate emergency and committed to improving public health,
biodiversity and active travel uptake across the
district.
 
7. A major commercial
development at Apperley Bridge on land owned by Yorkshire Water has
received planning permission and represents one of the largest
developments affecting the Idle and Thackley area.
 
This
Council believes that:
 
• Blue and green
infrastructure should be recognised as critical infrastructure and
treated with the same seriousness as transport, schools and
utilities.
 
• Development should
deliver measurable environmental and connectivity improvements
rather than simply mitigating harm, and are mandated to do so
through policies such as Biodiversity Net Gain, which requires a
10% BNG improvement either on-site or elsewhere through approved
payments.
 
• Dry-stone walls are
vital elements of the ward’s environmental and cultural
heritage.
 
• Safe, accessible active
travel routes are essential to delivering climate commitments and
healthy neighbourhoods.
 
·      
Sites such as St Ives Estate and the Bradford
Pennine Gateway represent huge blue green infrastructure
opportunities for the district, making significant contributions to
our environmental goals with the potential to attract investment
into the district and form part of our wider tourism and leisure
offer.
 
This
Council therefore resolves to:
 
1. Continue requiring robust
flood risk assessment and effective Sustainable Drainage Systems
for developments affecting the River Aire and canal
catchments.
 
2. Continue to pursue external
funding and developer contributions to support green and blue
infrastructure improvements, recognising that significant
investment has been made into the district already by doing
this.
 
3. Continue encouraging high
environmental standards and strong connections to the wider
ecological network for all new developments.
4. Encourage members to liaise
with our Active Travel team on potential active travel projects in
their ward so they can be assessed and considered for future
funding rounds.
 
5. Hold member workshops as
part of the development of the Bradford Transport Strategy, looking
specifically at local active travel networks.
 
6. Send the draft Transport
Strategy to the Regeneration and Environment Overview and Scrutiny
Committee for wider discussion with members.
7. Ask the cross-party Local
Plan Member Reference Group to hold a session on blue-green
infrastructure and how it will be represented and policies
regarding it strengthened in the Local Plan.
 
To be
actioned by:  Strategic Director Growth,
Interim Strategic Director of Environment

(i)            
SECTION
151 OFFICER ASSESSMENT UNDER S25 OF THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT 2003
OF THE COUNCIL'S FINANCIAL POSITION *
 
Resolved
–
 

(1)      That Council have
regard to Executive Document “BF” in setting the
budget, and in particular noted the conclusions that provided
that:
 

Ø 
the Government supports the Council with a
“minded to” Capitalisation Direction for financial year
2026/27;
 

Ø 
the recommendations in the budget reports be
agreed and actioned in full
 

Ø 
reserves continue to be built up as
required;
 

Ø 
risks are properly and promptly
managed;
 

Ø 
financial management issues are successfully
addressed;
 
then the
overall estimates are sufficiently robust for the Council to set a
balanced budget for 2026/27.
 
(2)      Council agreed:
 

Ø 
that the level of reserves be
increased;
 

Ø 
to implementation in full of the financial
strategy i.e. that the Council:
 

·       identifies an estimated £50m of revenue savings for
2027/28 and 2028/29;

·       identifies £100m of assets to be sold to generate capital
receipts, and investigates the potential for more;

·       operates expenditure control panels as set out in the report
until at least 2027/28;

·       continues with its review of financial management and finances
of the Council;

·       invests in core functions necessary and subject to business
cases;
 

Ø 
any non delivery of any planned revenue savings
will need to be absorbed within cash limited Departmental
budgets (in consultation with S151 Officer).

(3)      That Council noted:
 

Ø 
the assessment of the current financial position
of the Council;
 

Ø 
that this assessment is the result of emerging
and recent work. The situation will change and the estimated
financial position and solutions will require continual development
and refinement and will likewise vary as the year
progresses;
 

Ø 
the s151 officer is not minded to issue a s114
notice at this point working on the basis that the above
assumptions will be supported and seen through on time and in
full;
 

Ø 
given the extremely challenging financial
situation the Council finds itself in, which it has started to
address, if the recommendations are not agreed, or if the
assumptions are not delivered as assumed then very serious
consideration will be given to the issuing of a s114
notice;
 

Ø 
as with all budgets there is the potential for
amendments to be proposed/agreed which could change the overall
package of proposals. In that respect, it should be highlighted
that this statement would have to be amended if a decision was
proposed that leads to the Council’s budget not being in
balance. In addition, any other amendments would be considered
against the scale of the overall budget and depending upon the
extent and nature, may result in a revised
statement.

 
To be
actioned by: Interim Strategic Director of Corporate Resources/
S151 Officer
 
 
(ii)       MEDIUM-TERM
FINANCIAL STRATEGY (MTFS) 2026/27 TO 2030/31
 
Resolved
–
 
That
Council:
  

(1)          
Approvedthe updated
Medium-Term Financial Strategy for 2026/27 to 2030/31, including
the CD (Capitalisation Direction) request for 2026/27 and the
revised recovery period;

 

(2)          
Agreed the savings
target of £50m per annum from 2027/28 to 2028/29, currently
estimated to reduce to £40m from 2029/30;
 

(3)          
Agreed to receive an
updated MTFS in March 2026;
 

(4)          
Agreed the continued
spending panel and related control processes for a further two
years until the Council can evidence a sustainable financial
position and a track record of robust governance by
2028/29; 
 

(5)      Noted
that the key assumptions under pinning
the MTFS listed in paragraph 5.40 of Executive Document
“BG”;
 

(6)          
Noted that without
EFS (Exceptional Financial Support) which is subject to a review by
CIPFA and agreement by MHCLG the Council would not be able to set a
budget for 2026/27;
 

(7)          
Noted the current
position on the DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant), the likely Council
forecast for this and that it be agreed that further work be
undertaken.

 
To be actioned by: Interim
Strategic Director of Corporate Resources/ S151
Officer
 
(iii)     HOUSING REVENUE ACCOUNT 30-YEAR
BUSINESS PLAN AND   2026/27
BUDGET
 
Resolved
–
 
That
Council approved:
 

·  
the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) revenue budget
for 2026/7 (Table 2 – Paragraph 6.1 of Executive Document
“BH”)
 

·  
the HRA 5-year capital programme for a total of
£4.031m (Table – 3 of Executive Document
“BH”)
 
That
Council noted:
 

·  
the HRA 5-year revenue budgets for 2026-27 to
2030-31 (Table 2 –Paragraph 6.1 of Executive Document
“BH”)
 

·  
Average Rents, Social, Affordable & Extra
Care Housing (Appendix 1 to Executive Document
“BH”)
 

·  
the HRA 30-year revenue Business Plans for
2026-27 to 2055-56 (Appendix 2 to Executive Document
“BH”)
 

·  
the 30-year Major Repair and Improvement
programme for 2026-27 to 2055/6 (Appendix 3 to Executive Document
“BH”)
 

·  
the draft HRA reserves and balances for the
5-year business plan (Appendix 4 to Executive Document
“BH”)
 

·  
HRA Business Plan Risk Profile (Appendix 5 to
Executive Document “BH”)
 
To be
actioned by: Interim Strategic Director of Corporate Resources/
S151 Officer
 

 
 
 
(iv)     CAPITAL INVESTMENT PLAN 2026-27
TO 2030-31
 
Resolved
–
 

That Council:
 

Ø 
 Approved the Capital
Strategy (including Prudential Indicators) as set out at Section A
to Executive Document “BI”.
 

Ø 
 Approved the capital
expenditure for the General Fund and HRA as set out in Appendix D
to Executive Document “BI” for 2026-27 to 2030-31
subject to:
 

§ 
all future schemes being included in the Council
approved Capital Programme;

§ 
all new schemes, including third party funded,
only commencing with a full business case assessed via Project
Appraisal Group, Council Management Team (CMT) and approved by
Executive and subject to being in the Capital
Programme;

§ 
authority being given to the S151 Officer to
allow specific exceptions to the approval process when in their
opinion it is in the Council's interest. The S151 will keep a
record of these exceptions and report to Executive;

§ 
a further review of the capital programme, in
Summer 2026, and a report back to Executive; and

§ 
continued update on the capital receipts
potential, in the 2026/27 quarterly reports.
 

Ø 
Approved the
inclusion of the new capital requirements for 2026-27 onwards as
detailed in Appendix B and C to Executive Document “BI”
for inclusion in the programme and subject to the same as
above.
 

Ø  Approved that all projects follow
the approved business case governance process. Commitments against
reserve schemes and contingencies can only be made after a business
case has been assessed by Project Appraisal Group, CMT and approved
by Executive.
 

Ø   Approved
thatspecific approval be given for the
following schemes to commence following a review by Project
Appraisal Group:
 

§ 
The 2026-27 Property Programme has a proposed
total cost of £2m and this will be funded by £2m
allocated in Capital Reserve Schemes.

§ 
The 2026-27 BACES (Bradford & Airedale
Community Equipment Store) programme has a proposed cost of
£0.5m, and this will be funded by £0.5m allocated in
Capital Reserve Schemes.

§ 
£1.047m to complete proposed improvement
works at the Bradford Public Mortuary and Forensic Science Centre.
The funding is from Council corporate borrowing, but it is
anticipated that, in line with the funding for the wider
coroner’s service, contributions will be received from
Calderdale and Kirklees Councils.

§ 
£0.541m to carry out external refurbishment
works and replace flooring at the Alhambra Theatre. This will be
funded by corporate borrowing.
 

Ø 
Approved that no
financing sources, unless stipulated in regulations or necessary
agreements, are ring fenced.
 

Ø 
Approved the
proposed financing of the capital programme and revenue
implications as set out in the report (Document
“BI”).
 

Ø 
Delegated to the
Section 151 Officer the decisions surrounding financing of the
capital programme to provide sufficient flexibility to allow for
the most effective use of the Council’s
resources.
 
To be actioned by: Interim Strategic Director
of Corporate Resources/ S151 Officer
 
 
(v)      TREASURY MANAGEMENT
STRATEGY 2026/27
 
Resolved –
 
That
Council:
 

(1)         Approved
the Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27
including:

Ø 
the Minimum Revenue Provision Policy Statement
for 2026/27 (Appendix 1 to Executive Document “BJ”);
and

Ø 
the Annual Investment Strategy for 2026/27
(Appendix 2 to Executive Document “BJ”).

 

(2)          
Approved the
Prudential Indicators set out in the Treasury Management Strategy,
which demonstrate that the Council’s short term capital
investment plans are affordable, prudent and sustainable (the
Prudential Indicators are summarised in Section 4 of Executive
Document “BJ”).
 
To be actioned by: Interim Strategic Director
of Corporate Resources/ S151 Officer
 
 
(vi)     ALLOCATION OF THE SCHOOLS BUDGET
2026/27 FINANCIAL YEAR
 
Resolved
–
 
That
Council:
 

(1)      Accepted and
approved the proposals for the allocation of the 2026/27 Dedicated
Schools Grant, as set out in Executive Document
“BK”.
 

(2)      Approved the total
amount of £829.224m to be appropriated in respect of all
schools covered by the Bradford Scheme for the Local Management of
Schools, so as to establish the Individual Schools Budget for
2026/27.
 
To be
actioned by: Interim Strategic Director of Corporate Resources/
S151 Officer
 
 
(vii)    COUNCIL TAX REDUCTION SCHEME
2026/27
 
Resolved
–
 
That:

 

(1)           
Council considered and noted the outcome of the public consultation
as set out in Appendix 1 to Executive Document “BL” and
discussed in the body of the report.

 

(2)           
Members/Council have due regard to their responsibilities under the
Public Sector Equality Duty and consider the potential impacts of
the proposed changes as set out in the Equality Impact Assessment
in Appendix 2 to Executive Document “BL”.

 

(3)           
Council agreed that the proposed amendment to the Council Tax
Reduction Scheme to increase the maximum award from 70% of a Band A
property charge to 72.5% of a Band A property charge be adopted to
take effect from 1 April 2026 i.e. Option 1 as set out in Appendix
3 to Executive Document “BL”. 
 
To be
actioned by: Interim Strategic Director of Corporate Resources/
S151 Officer
 (viii)  THE COUNCIL'S REVENUE ESTIMATES FOR 2026-27
(GENERAL   FUND)
 
Resolved –
 
2026-27
REVENUE BUDGET ESTIMATES

 

(1)          
That the Base Revenue Estimated Budget of
£737.369m for 2026-27 be approved as set out in Appendix A to
Executive Document “BM”;

That within the Base Revenue Estimated Budget of
£737.369m for 2026-27, the Departmental Net Expenditure

“BM”;

That amounts for Inflationary Uplifts to
Departmental Net Expenditure Budgets of £35.0m in 2026-27 as
set out in Appendix E to Executive Document “BM” be
approved;

 

(5)          
That amounts for Time Limited investments of
£6.100m in 2026-27 as set out in Appendix F to Executive
Document “BM” be approved;

 

(6)          
That amounts for reserve movements of
£20.750m in 2026-27 as set out in Appendix G to Executive
Document “BM” be approved;

 

(7)          
 That savings proposals
for 2026-27 totalling £60.6m as previously agreed at the
Executive on 4th
November 2025 and as set out below be
approved;

Ø  5 proposals totalling
£9.8m (Section 9.5 to 9.11),

Ø  6 budget realignment
proposals totalling £3.2m, (Section 9.12 to
9.17),  

Ø  4 Corporate Savings

(8)          
That the confirmation included in Appendix I to
Executive Document “BM” of the in-principal
capitalisation support for 2026-27 of £78m by the Minister
for Local Government and Homelessness be noted.

 

(9)          
That the comments of the Interim Strategic
Director of Corporate Resources /s151 Officer set out in a separate
report (Section 151 officer’s assessment of the proposed
budgets on the robustness of the estimates and the adequacy of
reserves - Executive Document “BF”) taking account of
the recommendations made  above be
noted.

 

DELEGATION TO OFFICERS

 

(10)      
That the s151 Officer be granted delegated
authority to approve requests for time-limited investment in
consultation with the Chief Executive.

 

(11)      
That the s151 Officer be granted delegated
authority to approve requests to allocate items of growth held
centrally to departments in consultation with the Chief Executive
including new burdens associated with:

 

a. the Extender Producer Responsibility
grant

b. the Crisis and Resilience Fund

c. the Children, Families and Youth Grant

d. the Homelessness, Rough Sleeping and Domestic
Abuse grant   

e. the Public Health grant.
 

(12)      
That the S151 officer be given authority to make
reductions to growth and pressure items and utilisation of
contingency in consultation with the Chief Executive if on-going
monitoring indicates it is prudent to do so. Any changes to be
reported to the Executive.

 

(13)      
That for the avoidance of doubt and without
prejudice to any of the powers contained in Article 14 of Part 2 of
the Council's Constitution on the Function of Officers: the s151
Officer shall have delegated authority to act on behalf of the
Council on matters relating to Council Tax, Non-Domestic Rates and
Accounts Receivable Debtors including (without prejudice to the
generality of the delegation) entry into any business rate pools,
pilots, assessments, determinations, recovery, enforcement and, in
accordance with the statutory scheme, full delegated powers to act
on behalf of the Council with regard to all aspects of the granting
of Discretionary and Hardship Rate Relief to qualifying
ratepayers.
 

 

(14)      
That the s151 Officer be given authority to
secure the best position for the Council in respect of 2025-26 in
preparing the Final Accounts for 2025-26, noting that the financial
position is contingent upon the 2025-26 audited
out-turn.
 

PAYMENT DATES FOR COUNCIL TAX AND NATIONAL
NON-DOMESTIC

RATES
 

(15)       
That the S151 Officer be given authority to
specify the first instalment date for payment of Council Tax and
National Non-Domestic Rates
 

PROPOSED COUNCIL TAX 2026-27
 

(16)       
That it be noted that the projected Council Tax
base and expenditure forecasts outlined in the report  together with the 2026-27 resources and the budget
variations approved in the recommendations above produce a proposed
Band D Council Tax of £1,965.28 for 2026-27. This is a
£93.40 (4.99%) increase from 2025-26 in line with the bespoke
referendum limit approved for the Council by the Minister for Local
Government and English Devolution.

content:
The report provides the view of the S151
Officer on the robustness of the proposed budget for
2026-27,  the adequacy of forecast
levels of reserves and associated risks.

Resolved –
 
That
it be recommended to Council:
 

(1)      That Members have
regard to this report in setting the budget, and in particular note
the conclusions that provided that:
 
Ø 
the Government supports the Council with a “minded to”
Capitalisation Direction for financial year 2026/27;
 
Ø 
the recommendations in this and the other budget reports are agreed
and actioned in full
 
Ø 
reserves continue to be built up as required;
 
Ø 
risks are
properly and promptly managed;
 
Ø 
financial management issues are successfully addressed;
 
then
the overall estimates are sufficiently robust for the Council to
set a balanced budget for 2026/27.
 
(2)      That Members agree:
 
Ø 
that the
level of reserves be increased;
 
Ø 
to implementation in full of the financial strategy ie that the Council:
 
·      
identifies an estimated £50m of revenue
savings for 2027/28 and 2028/29;
·      
identifies £100m of assets to be sold to
generate capital receipts, and investigates the potential for
more;
·      
operates expenditure control panels as set out in
the report until at least 2027/28;
·      
continues with its review of financial management
and finances of the Council;
·      
invests in core functions necessary and subject
to business cases;
 
Ø 
any non delivery of any planned revenue
savings will need to be absorbed within 
cash limited Departmental budgets (in consultation with
S151).


(3)      That Members note:
 
Ø 
the assessment of the current financial position of the Council;
 
Ø 
that this
assessment is the result of emerging and recent work. The
situation will change and the estimated financial position and
solutions will require continual development and refinement and
will likewise vary as the year progresses;
 
Ø 
the s151
officer is not minded to issue a s114
notice at this point working on the basis that the above
assumptions will be supported and seen through on time and in
full;
 
Ø 
given the
extremely challenging financial situation the Council finds itself
in, which it has started to address, if the recommendations are not
agreed, or if the assumptions are not delivered as assumed then
very serious consideration will be given to the issuing of a s114
notice;
 
Ø 
as with all
budgets there is the potential for amendments to be proposed/agreed
which could change the overall package of proposals. In that
respect, it should be highlighted that this statement would have to
be amended if a decision was proposed that leads to the
Council’s budget not being in balance. In addition, any other
amendments would be considered against the scale of the overall
budget and depending upon the extent and nature, may result in a
revised statement.

 
To be actioned
by: Interim Strategic Director of
Corporate Resources / S151
 
Overview and Scrutiny Area:
Corporate                                
 
(Steven Mair)

content:
To present the final draft of the Children and
Young People’s Strategy. The Strategy is a chapter of the
District Plan and sets out what partners will do to improve the
lives of children, young people and families to help make Bradford
District a great place to grow up.

Recommended –
 
(1)             
That the progress that has been made during the
life span of the Children and Young People’s Strategy 2023
– 2025 be noted.
 
(2)             
That the approach taken with the development of
the new Strategy 2025 - 2035, enabling annual monitoring of
District-wide outcomes for all children and young people, and
termly monitoring of five priority areas of work be
noted.
 
(3)

content:
Resolved-
 
Having considered all
valid representations made by the parties at the hearing, the valid
written representations received during the statutory consultation
period, the Council’s published Statement of Licensing
Policy, the Licensing Act 2003 (in particular sections 37 and
42 concerning applications to vary a premises licence to
specify a designated premises supervisor and to transfer a premises
licence respectively), and the relevant statutory guidance
issued under section 182 of the Licensing Act 2003, the Panel
is satisfied that granting the applications to transfer the
premises licence and to vary the premises licence to specify the
applicant as the Designated Premises Supervisor  for Jimmy’s, 97 Great Horton Road, Bradford,
BD7 1PS would undermine the licensing objectives, in particular
the prevention of crime and disorder. 
 
Reasons:
 

Members have
carefully considered the representations and evidence before them,
including the history of criminal offending that led to the
revocation of the previous premises licence.


 

In the view of
the Panel, the available evidence provides insufficient
assurance Members therefore have no confidence that the criminal
offending would not be repeated.

 

 

The Panel finds
that the risk of recurrence of matters undermining
the prevention of crime and disorder objective is such that it
would be inappropriate to grant either the transfer of the premises
licence under section 42 of the Licensing Act 2003 or the variation
to specify the applicant as Designated Premises Supervisor under
section 37 of that Act.

 
For these reasons, the
Licensing Panel refuses the application to transfer the
premises licence and refuses the application to vary the premises
licence to specify the applicant as the Designated Premises
Supervisor.
 
To be
actioned by: Assistant Director Stronger Communities and Regulatory
Services
topline: The Council has decided to refuse the application to transfer the premises licence and refuse the application to vary the premises licence for Jimmy's in Bradford.

Resolved –
 
That the

(1)          
Noted the current forecast positions and
supported the     continued
management of the Council’s budgets.
 

(2)          
Approved the following new capital
expenditure schemes as outlined in section 10.6 to Document
“BC”, namely:
 
Sir Henry
Mitchell House (SHMH) Building Improvements - £0.649m:
Building improvements required at SHMH, the corporate headquarters
and designated building for most Bradford Children and Families
Trust (BCFT) staff.  The improvements
will create a more suitable working environment, including
additional space for meetings and conferences which are lacking in
the existing building configuration. 
The cost of the works will be funded from contingency
budgets.
 
Swimming
Pool Infrastructure Renewal - £0.636m: Capital works at four
of the Councils swimming pools: Eccleshill Pool, Ilkley Pool &
Lido, Shipley Pool, and Bowling Pool. 
The extent of the proposed works to maintain these pools varies
across the four sites, with the most substantive items of
expenditure including the removal and replacement of filter
vessels, grouting of the swimming pools, inlet pipe replacement
(Ilkley Pool & Lido), balance tank repairs (Bowling Pool) and
the supply and fitting of UPVC windows and socket trunking
(Eccleshill Pool).
 
Family Hubs
Start for Life Programme - £0.136m: A series of projects to
support the transformation of family hubs to meet the needs of
families across the district and reach the most vulnerable
communities.  The programme comprises
projects at Shipley Library Garden, Barkerend Birth Registration
& Sensory Room, Farcliffe Sensory Garden, Reevy Sensory Room,
and the addition of a second portacabin at Thornaby Hub,
Clayton.  The work will be entirely
funded by ring-fenced grant from the Department for
Education.

 
Group Fitness Exercise Bikes – £0.060m: The purchase
of 57 commercial-standard exercise
bikes for use across three Council-owned sport and leisure
facilities: Thornton Recreation Centre, Eccleshill Pool, and
Sedbergh Sports and Leisure Centre. The bikes will replace existing
units that, primarily due to their age no longer meet the required
standards.  The proposal will be funded
through borrowing, with repayments made via annual revenue
contributions from existing budgets.       
 
Haworth
Road Play Area Outdoor Gym – £0.055m: The provision of
an outdoor gym at Haworth Road Play Area.  Funding for the project will comprise a
combination of external grant funding (£0.031m) and Community
Infrastructure Levy (£0.024m).

 
Shearbridge
Depot Workshop Extraction System – £0.050m: A new
workshop extraction system at Shearbridge Depot to replace an
existing system which is no longer at the required
standard.  The acquisition will be met
from contingency budgets.
 
Bowling
Back Lane Transfer Station Weighbridge – £0.042m: A new
weighbridge at Bowling Back Lane Transfer Station to allow for the
weighing in and out of waste and recyclables.  The current weighbridge is at risk of failure and
has been deemed to be beyond economic repair.  The acquisition will be met from contingency
budgets.
 
Bolling
Hall Museum Wheelchair Lift – £0.018m: The installation
of a wheelchair lift at Bolling Hall Museum, to enable full step
free access to the lower floors of the premises for visitors with
mobility impairments.  The cost of the
works will be met from contingency budgets.
 
Discretionary Disabled Facilities Grants -
£0.105m: Adaptations to 3 carers homes to enable children
with disabilities supported by the Bradford Children’s and
Families Trust to continue to be supported in their own
homes.
 

(3)

Section 5.31 of the Financial Regulations, as outlined in
  section         10.7 to
Document “BC”:
 
Infrastructure Works Bodies of Water - £0.150m: Works to
